channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: Written for a grandson, new hymn ‘Close as a Quiet Prayer’ teaches truth to all children
item.description: Songwriter Sally DeFord wrote the new hymn "Close as a Quiet Prayer" for a grandson, though its message is meant for all children. She traced its roots to a Primary poster her son once taped inside his closet door, which affirmed that he was a child of God who could pray to Heavenly Father at any time and place. DeFord told the Church News she counts it a blessing that God is never distant and always hears prayer. The Deseret News page is a short excerpt, and the complete Church News feature is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church makes $1 million campaign contribution to oppose abortion ballot measure in Idaho
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has given $1 million to Too Extreme for Idaho, the PAC fighting Proposition 1, an Idaho ballot measure that would create a state right to abortion ahead of the Nov. 3 election. A spokesperson for the opposition campaign revealed the gift on an Idaho Falls radio show, and the church confirmed it in a statement saying it stays neutral on candidates but weighs in on ballot questions it sees as morally significant. The donation boosts the PAC's cash on hand by nearly 40%, though its roughly $2.68 million raised still trails the $4.5 million collected by the measure's backers, Idahoans United for Women and Families. Deseret News reporter Tad Walch notes that the church had letters read in about 1,300 Idaho congregations in September and is also opposing a similar ratification vote in Nevada.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: ‘Act of healing’: Church’s donation to help Grandmother of Juneteenth amplify Black voices
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is donating $3 million toward the planned National Juneteenth Museum in Fort Worth, Texas, including a FamilySearch-backed Genealogy Center with oral history recording booths. The gift was celebrated at a site-clearing event coinciding with the 100th birthday of Opal Lee, the activist known as the Grandmother of Juneteenth, who asked for the booths after touring the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City. Elder Michael A. Dunn, a General Authority Seventy, said the First Presidency approved the donation as part of an effort to recover African American family histories obscured by slavery, and museum CEO Jarred Howard praised the church's long partnership. Deseret News reporter Tad Walch writes that the church also delivered a truckload of food to Fort Worth pantries during the event.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Trimmed talks: Charts show how Latter-day Saint leaders found time for more conference speakers
item.description: In his ChurchBeat newsletter, Deseret News reporter Tad Walch charts how shorter talks have let The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints squeeze more speakers into general conference. The October 2026 conference featured 37 speakers, compared with 34 at each of the previous two, and twice fit 10 speakers into one session, a high for at least 50 years. Talks by the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve shrank from an average of nearly 15 minutes in October 2025 to under 12 minutes, while other speakers' talks are about a quarter shorter, with one running about seven and a half minutes. Extra time also came from skipping a solemn assembly and the auditing report and from a briefer sustaining of officers.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church-endorsed chaplains feel loved, ‘seen’ by Church leaders at annual seminar
item.description: Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told chaplains endorsed by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints at the 2026 Chaplain Training Seminar that the First Presidency and the Twelve pray for them. The Church News item centers on Karina Cooksey, a mother of five and now a second lieutenant and chaplain candidate in the U.S. Air Force Reserve. Cooksey said she felt God led her to that path despite her early reluctance, and that the apostle's message comforted her. The Deseret News page has only a short excerpt; the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Sister Runia testifies to missionaries of 3 things that are true
item.description: Sister Tamara W. Runia, first counselor in the Young Women general presidency, spoke at the Provo Missionary Training Center on Tuesday, Oct. 6. She told the missionaries that some truths can be invisible, hard to understand or seem too good to be true and still be true, and shared a letter from a young adult who was regaining lost hope. Quoting Alma 5:12, she encouraged them to share that same assurance with the people they teach. The Deseret News page carries only an excerpt of this Church News report; the full account is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Get tickets to join this celebration of faith and Latino cultures
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will hold its 24th Luz de las Naciones celebration of Latin American music and dance on Nov. 13-14 at 8 p.m. in Salt Lake City's Conference Center, and for the first time it will include African and African American performances. About 1,000 volunteers will perform traditions from countries including Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Mexico, Peru, Spain and Venezuela, and show director Israel González-Nieri said more countries are represented than ever. Last year, President Dallin H. Oaks became the first sitting church president to attend in person. Admission is free but requires tickets, which become available Oct. 13 at 10 a.m., and the Nov. 14 show will stream in Spanish on ChurchofJesusChrist.org, Amy Ortiz reports.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: New docuseries invites viewers to bring their faith — and questions — to the Salt Lake Temple open house
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints premiered "Dedicate" on Sunday, a six-part docuseries that follows seven young adults from Brazil, France, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines and the U.S. as they prepare to see the renovated Salt Lake Temple. At a Monday screening, President Emily Belle Freeman said none of the conversations were scripted, and Elder Gary E. Stevenson said the series was made for the rising generation. The first episode includes participants' doubts, with recent convert Sora Murata of Japan and Alexandra Hovermale of Alabama saying filming changed how they see the temple. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf called the launch part of a worldwide celebration ahead of the temple's April 5-Oct. 1, 2027 open house, and new episodes will roll out in the coming weeks, Amy Ortiz reports.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Is Anthropic a new religion?
item.description: In her State of Faith newsletter, Mariya Manzhos looks at a New York Times report that AI company Anthropic has been meeting with Sikh, Catholic, evangelical and other religious thinkers while taking seriously the possibility that its Claude models could be conscious. According to the Times, co-founder Christopher Olah spoke with Elder Gerrit W. Gong, and a rabbi at one dinner said company staff seemed to grant Claude moral status, though Olah said he is "genuinely uncertain" whether AI is conscious. Manzhos contrasts that openness with firm religious objections: Pope Leo XIV rejects the idea that AI can be conscious, and Elder Gong has said that "AI is math" and is not alive. Catholic scholar Luke Burgis turned down an invitation to the meetings, worrying that religious voices would add credibility rather than real influence. Manzhos ends with open questions about who is accountable if increasingly autonomous AI causes harm.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: A look at the progress, process and power of the ongoing, sacred project to update the Church’s music collection
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has now released 82 new songs in English, Spanish, Portuguese and French as part of the music-collection overhaul the First Presidency announced in 2018, with more still planned. The effort replaces collections last revised in the 1980s: the 1985 hymnbook and the 1989 "Children's Songbook." This Church News item on the Deseret News site is a brief pointer to a longer feature on TheChurchNews.com about how the project is progressing.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: New statue of resurrected Jesus Christ unveiled inside Conference Center
item.description: A Michael Hall sculpture, "Christ Visits the Americas," now stands in the Conference Center atrium where a fountain used to be, and the 34,438 people at Saturday's two general conference sessions were the first members of the public to see it. Bill Williams, design director for Temples and Special Projects, said the old fountain was damaged in the 2020 earthquake and later leaked into the concrete, and church leaders used the replacement to make the building's art more focused on the Savior. The statue shows the resurrected Christ displaying his wounds as described in 3 Nephi 11, with verse 11 lettered on the wall above, and will be part of Conference Center tours during next year's Salt Lake Temple Celebration, which could draw 5 million visitors. Hall also sculpted two other recent Temple Square statues, Tad Walch writes in his ChurchBeat newsletter.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ will soon prepare grounds for this Arizona temple
item.description: No groundbreaking date has been set for the Yuma Arizona Temple, but the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints says crews will begin grading and laying underground utilities at the nearly seven-acre site once the city signs off, while design work continues. The single-story, roughly 18,500-square-foot temple will sit close to both the California and Mexico borders. It was Arizona's seventh announced temple when revealed in April 2024 and will serve a state with about 450,000 members, Amy Ortiz writes for the Deseret News.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Latter-day Saint general conference sets new speaker records
item.description: In his ChurchBeat newsletter, Tad Walch tallies the just-ended October 2026 general conference at 37 talks by 36 people, with President Dallin H. Oaks speaking twice, records for a conference held in the newer four-session format. He notes that two sessions featured 10 speakers apiece, something he found had not occurred once in the past century. The speakers came from 16 countries and one U.S. territory, which Walch says also appears to be a record. The comparison point is April's conference, the first with only four sessions, which matched the prior October's 34 talks despite losing a session.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: God can change any heart, starting with our own, Latter-day Saint leaders teach
item.description: Writing for the Deseret News, Jacob Hess argues that the weekend's 196th Semiannual General Conference was notably personal, with Latter-day Saint leaders focusing on how God's love reshapes individual hearts rather than on policy or politics. He gathers examples across speakers: Elder Ulisses Soares on fasting as a way to align one's will with God's, Elder Ronald A. Rasband urging members to entrust loved ones who have left the faith to Christ, and Elder Patrick Kearon's glider metaphor about finding lift and avoiding sink. President D. Todd Christofferson's call to put gambling out of members' lives entirely and Elder David A. Bednar's teaching on covenants also feature. Hess closes with Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota, Elder Hutch U. Fale and Young Men President Timothy L. Farnes on seeing others as God sees them and on a love that cannot be earned or lost.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: A large majority of surveyed Americans value ‘being a child of God’
item.description: BYU's Wheatley Institute released the first of four reports from its "Survey of Lived Religion," finding that 71% of Americans call being a child of God at least moderately important, well above the 55% who say the same of political identity. Authors Shima Baughman, Stephen Cranney and Paul Lambert designed the nationally representative survey to probe private practice rather than attendance alone, finding that 73% have sensed God speaking to them and 77% thank God monthly. Among religiously unaffiliated respondents, about three-quarters are open to some form of life after death and nearly half believe objects or places can hold spiritual power. The study also found that about half of Christians skipped Easter services last year and that only a third of religious Americans recall changing a decision in the past month because of prayer, Jacob Hess reports.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Who is a child of God? Latter-day Saint president declares distinctive beliefs at conference
item.description: Tad Walch's wrap-up of general conference's final day centers on distinctive doctrines President Dallin H. Oaks restated, including that further revelations will come to light recording Christ's ministry to other peoples, such as the lost tribes of Israel. Several talks returned to the teaching that every person is a literal child of God, a view many Christian traditions reject even though a Wheatley Institute poll found 71% of Americans hold it; Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota and Elder Gary E. Stevenson both stressed it. Elder David A. Bednar described the temple sealing of husband and wife as a crowning ordinance, and President Dieter F. Uchtdorf said shared covenants, not politics or culture, make members one people. Elder Clark G. Gilbert offered five principles drawn from President Oaks for standing up for truth with love, among them avoiding contentious settings and seeking common ground. Oaks also invited the public to tour the Salt Lake Temple during a six-month open house beginning April 5.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: President Oaks spoke about the ‘Dedicate’ series during general conference. Here’s what you need to know
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks ended the church's October 2026 general conference by pointing members to "Dedicate," a six-episode video series that premiered on the church's YouTube channel once the conference wrapped up. It follows seven young adults from Brazil, the Philippines, France, the United States, Japan, Ghana and Mexico as they meet leaders such as President Dieter F. Uchtdorf and Elder Neil L. Andersen, with the final episode walking through the renovated Salt Lake Temple. A trailer released Sept. 21 features participants from Ghana and France describing what the temple means to them. Joel Randall reports the series is part of the buildup to the temple's public open house from April 5 to Oct. 1, 2027, alongside free ticket releases on TempleSquare.org, guided and self-guided virtual tours, and a new music album.
item.dc:creator: Joel Randall

item.title: The gospel and grace of Jesus Christ are for everyone, Latter-day Saint president says
item.description: In the final talk of conference's Sunday morning session, President Dallin H. Oaks drew on the Book of Mormon to argue that God's grace extends to everyone rather than a chosen few, days before marking a year as the church's 18th president. He spoke directly to members whose faith is fading, saying church leaders and the Lord keep reaching for them, and counseled against letting secular learning narrow spiritual horizons while building faith through daily prayer, scripture study, the weekly sacrament and temple worship. Earlier speakers took up hardship: President Henry B. Eyring explained why God lets life be difficult and asked members to help answer others' prayers, and Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota taught the African greeting "Sawubona" and challenged listeners to learn the name of someone who feels unseen. Elder Quentin L. Cook tied happiness to integrity and called online bullying reprehensible, while Elder Neil L. Andersen spoke about courage rooted in faith, Tad Walch reports.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Apostle denounces gambling at Saturday morning session of general conference
item.description: President D. Todd Christofferson used the opening session of the October 2026 general conference to state plainly that the church opposes gambling. He cited President Dallin H. Oaks' 1987 teaching that trying to take something without giving value harms a person spiritually, and he noted that 2.3 billion adults worldwide gambled in the past year. Elder Gerrit W. Gong called temples places of peace amid commotion, as the church prepares to dedicate 21 this year, its second-highest total ever. Elder Gérald Caussé urged members to share their own testimonies, and Elder Ulisses Soares spoke about the power of fasting. Tad Walch reports that 16,996 people attended, and Bishop Sean Douglas said missionary service and baptisms are at all-time highs.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Trust Christ’s ability to love, lift and give peace, but don’t gamble, Latter-day Saint leaders say
item.description: Tad Walch's wrap-up of Saturday at the 196th Semiannual General Conference contrasts President D. Todd Christofferson's morning denunciation of gambling with an afternoon focused on Christ's love. Christofferson took on sports betting, online casinos and prediction markets and called gambling morally wrong. He noted U.S. sports wagers grew from $4.9 billion in 2017 to $160 billion in 2025, and in footnotes he described lotteries as a regressive tax. Elder Ronald A. Rasband told members aching over loved ones who left the faith to let go of guilt but not of those people, while Sister Tamara W. Runia drew on her son's sudden death to talk about how adversity shapes people. The article puts the 18 speakers in the context of record church growth, including 90,000 missionaries, 506 missions and 385,490 convert baptisms last year.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Live coverage of October 2026 general conference
item.description: The Deseret News and Church News live blog of the October 2026 general conference posts updates as each speaker and musical number finishes. Saturday afternoon entries cover Elder Ronald A. Rasband on loving family members who drift from the faith and Elder Patrick Kearon comparing spiritual growth to riding thermals in the gliders he flew as a teen. Elder Michael A. Dunn recounted a 100-mile ultramarathon, and Elder Jeremiah J. Morgan described his conversion after growing up in Community of Christ in Independence, Missouri. Entries add speakers' backgrounds, hymn histories and lyrics, and Sister J. Annette Dennis closed the session with the benediction. Sessions resume Sunday at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Jane Weaver, Caitlin Keith, Amy Ortiz and Leah Bowers

item.title: October 2026 general conference: Talk summaries, photos
item.description: Every talk from the October 2026 general conference of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints gets its own summary link on this Deseret News hub, which also collects photos and viewing information for the four sessions at Salt Lake City's Conference Center. Saturday's sessions featured 17 talks, from Elder Gerrit W. Gong and President D. Todd Christofferson in the morning to Elders Dale G. Renlund, Patrick Kearon and Ronald A. Rasband in the afternoon. The 196th Semiannual General Conference is the first October gathering since Dallin H. Oaks became church president nearly a year ago. The byline belongs to Deseret News managing editor Aaron Shill.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Shill

item.title: First child to speak about Grand Blanc shooting has some good advice
item.description: In this ChurchBeat newsletter excerpt, Tad Walch talks with Lincoln Brooks, 12, the first child to speak publicly about last year's attack on a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse in Grand Blanc, Michigan. After the gunman killed four people and set the building ablaze, Lincoln hid with his mother and sisters in a smoke-filled room until his mother, Katie Brooks, threw him out a window to rescuers, and the family later found his father, Rick, alive. Lincoln says his recovery started that night playing with a neighbor's dog. It continued when a cross-country teammate dropped back to run beside him, and when classmates at a school where he's the only church member kept checking in on him. He wants people to know how much that kind of connection has helped.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: How President Dallin H. Oaks is leading Latter-day Saints through a ‘glorious season of temple building’
item.description: Nearly a year after President Dallin H. Oaks was ordained on Oct. 14, 2025, Deseret News finds his tenure defined less by new temple announcements, which he deliberately slowed, than by faster progress on the 163 temples already in the pipeline out of the church's 385 total. Thirteen temples have been dedicated in his first year, two of them by Oaks himself in Burley, Idaho, and Belo Horizonte, Brazil, and 2026 is on track to rank second only to 2000, when 34 were dedicated. The First Presidency has also shifted announcements to local leaders, naming new temples in Portland, Maine; Marysville, Washington; and Otavalo, Ecuador. The dedications in Harare, Zimbabwe, and Alabang, Philippines, completed the last temples announced under President Thomas S. Monson, and the article closes with a status list for every temple still under way as of Oct. 1.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ donates over $7 million to American Red Cross
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is giving the American Red Cross more than $7 million for blood collection and disaster response, along with $850,000 for western Pacific communities hit by Super Typhoon Sinlaku in April. Bishop W. Christopher Waddell of the Presiding Bishopric framed the gift as caring for neighbors, Red Cross CEO Cliff Holtz praised the church's long partnership, and Utah/Nevada regional CEO Heidi Ruster said a Murray investment will expand capacity in the state. The relationship traces back to correspondence between Clara Barton and Relief Society leader Emmeline B. Wells in the 1890s, and since its first blood drive in 1996 the church has become the single largest contributor to Red Cross drives. Previous gifts totaled $5.1 million last year and $7.35 million in 2024, and the church reported $1.58 billion in welfare and humanitarian spending in 2025.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Can fighters be peacemakers? Inside the minds of Christians in MMA
item.description: With the UFC holding 14 fights at Salt Lake City's Delta Center on Saturday, Oct. 3, while Latter-day Saints meet a few blocks away for general conference, Deseret News asked whether cage fighting fits with Christian discipleship and peacemaking. The piece notes a wave of on-air faith declarations in 2026, including middleweight Bo Nickal quoting scripture at a White House card watched by 34 million, Mauricio Ruffy urging viewers to give their lives to Jesus, and Jalin Turner telling a UFC 330 crowd that a revival is under way. Podcaster and amateur fighter Cade Alvey argued that fighting and peacemaking rarely collide and that MMA gyms can be friendlier than rec-league softball. Pro and local fighters interviewed described treating bouts as sport rather than hatred, using the microphone to share their faith, and finding that the suffering of training draws them closer to Christ, with one comparing restrained force to the Book of Mormon account of Ammon.
item.dc:creator: Krysyan Edler and Aaron Shill

item.title: A tale of 2 temples: The reconstruction and slight relocation of the Anchorage Alaska Temple
item.description: For roughly the next five months, the two closest temples of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are both in Anchorage, Alaska: the original Anchorage Alaska Temple and its replacement, being built about 80 yards away. That gap beats the long-standing record holders in Utah, where the Provo City Center and Provo Utah Rock Canyon temples have sat about 2.3 miles apart since 2014. The Church News piece examines the rebuild and small move of the Alaska temple. Deseret News runs only a brief excerpt, and the full story is on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ names new Area Seventy in leadership meeting
item.description: Elder David Kannar, 64, of Queensland, Australia, was sustained as a new Area Seventy during the leadership meeting held Thursday ahead of the October 2026 general conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. He will serve in the Eighth Quorum of the Seventy, which covers the Pacific and Philippines areas, replacing Elder Robert H. Simpson, who had served since April 2021. Kannar and his wife, Sally-Jane, have four children and previously led the Cameroon Yaoundé Mission. Area Seventies, called by the First Presidency, typically serve part-time for about five years while keeping their regular jobs.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: How the Church turned competition into collaboration for 8 global humanitarian organizations
item.description: Faced with humanitarian groups that often compete with each other for donors, government aid and volunteers, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has paired eight of them into four consortia that share the work. The arrangement is part of the Caring for Women and Children Initiative, which the church expanded in 2024 and which targets 12 high-need countries such as Nepal, Nigeria and Kenya. One group of three partners concentrates on nutrition and medicine, supplying supplements, vitamins and more nourishing food. The Church News report is a short preview, and the full article is posted on TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Keith McMullin, former CEO of Deseret Management, dies at age 85
item.description: Keith B. McMullin, former member of the Presiding Bishopric of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and CEO of Deseret Management Corp. from 2012 to 2023, died Wednesday at age 85. H. David Burton, who served alongside him in the bishopric for nearly 20 years, described a leader who weighed every decision by its effect on people, and DMC executives Sheri Dew and Gary Porter recalled him as a gracious boss and wise mentor. Born in St. George in 1941, McMullin studied finance at the University of Utah, worked at Ford Motor Co. and spent two decades in church welfare services before his 1995 bishopric call. He saw his business career as part of his faith, and he was honored with two Utah business awards in 2024.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Institute celebrates its 100th anniversary on the date and at the place where it all began
item.description: Moscow, Idaho, home of the University of Idaho, is where the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' Institutes of Religion program began a century ago, and it is also where the centennial was marked. Church President Heber J. Grant sent J. Wyley Sessions there on Sept. 26, 1926, to start "collegiate seminaries," with no building or curriculum and an initial class of 25 students. The Deseret News page is a brief excerpt, and Church News has the full report on the commemoration.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Why we all need more rituals
item.description: In this State of Faith newsletter essay, Mariya Manzhos describes a workshop at the Restore conference led by Casper ter Kuile, author of "The Power of Ritual" and former co-host of the podcast "Harry Potter and the Sacred Text." Ter Kuile, who is not religious, said rituals give people "a home in time," and he distinguished a ritual from a routine by its intention and meaning, adding that even a skin-care routine can work as a memento mori. Participants traded inventive family traditions and drew up a yearly ritual calendar, which led Manzhos, who grew up with few family traditions, to conclude that her life already had enough rituals but lacked deliberate preparation and a story behind them. The newsletter also looks at why heavily secular France gave Pope Leo XIV a huge welcome, noting that only 8% of French adults attend church.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Former NYT columnist makes a case for God and religion
item.description: Ross Douthat, a Catholic writer who spent 17 years as a New York Times columnist and now reports for "60 Minutes," told a BYU forum audience Tuesday that everyone should be religious. He finally made it after a February snowstorm and a second weather threat had delayed his visit, and joked that either dark powers or God was sending him a message. Douthat said no single argument proves God exists, but several lines of evidence together make belief reasonable: physical constants finely tuned for life, the mystery of human consciousness, and spiritual experience that has persisted even as institutional religion has weakened. He urged believers to live their faith with confidence rather than embarrassment, and he develops the case further in his book "Believe: Why Everyone Should Be Religious."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Temple Square is transforming. Here’s what you can see right now
item.description: With the Salt Lake Temple nearing the end of a renovation of almost seven years, the Deseret News outlines which parts of Temple Square visitors can see now and which remain closed. The temple itself is still closed, but the surrounding gates and walkways have reopened, so visitors can get close to its 19th-century exterior; Welfare Square and the new Humanitarian Center nearby are also open for tours. The Conference Center will reopen briefly for general conference on Oct. 3-4 and a few other events before closing again through March 1, 2027. Public temple tours will run April 5 through Oct. 1 next year, and the next batch of tickets opens Oct. 1 at 6 p.m. MDT.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Latter-day Saints share honors for interfaith efforts and charity at Boston Red Sox game
item.description: Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Boston gathered at Fenway Park on Wednesday, Sept. 23, for a Latter-day Saint Night that doubled as a recognition of local community and interfaith work. The Red Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 1-0 that evening. Four honorees were recognized on the field before the game: Matthew Christensen, who previously led the Cambridge Massachusetts Stake; the Rev. Mark Scott, associate pastor of the Azusa Christian Community; Pastor Reba Danastorg of Imani Temple Church of God in Christ; and Dr. Gordon Williams, a Harvard medical professor and Latter-day Saint. Church News, which reported the event, directs readers to TheChurchNews.com for its full account.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ advances first international temple announced under President Oaks
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has settled on a site for the Otavalo Ecuador Temple, the first international temple announced under church President Dallin H. Oaks and the first of his three announced temples to have a site map released. The First Presidency said the temple will occupy a 6.05-acre parcel on the outskirts of Otavalo in northern Ecuador and will run roughly 18,850 square feet. The temple was announced less than six months ago, on May 14, during a devotional for local members, with the First Presidency calling it a reason to rejoice and a blessing that would give members more frequent access to temple ordinances and covenants. The Portland Maine and Marysville Washington temples, also announced under President Oaks, remain in planning and design. The First Presidency separately announced that groundbreaking for the Cuernavaca Mexico Temple — one of 27 in that country — will be held Saturday, Nov. 14, presided over by Elder Moises Villanueva, president of the church's Mexico Area.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: A year after the Grand Blanc church shooting, survivors cling to faith as memory haunts them
item.description: A year after a man drove a pickup into the front wall of a Latter-day Saint chapel in Grand Blanc, Michigan, and opened fire on 215 worshippers, survivors told the Deseret News that recovery has been neither quick nor linear. Dawn Sheik, a middle school math teacher with active shooter training, was among the first to move, turning to her daughters and then to the rows around her to shout at people to run, while Bishop Jeffrey Schaub reached the microphone and directed everyone out the back doors. Congregation members want the four who died named first, calling them the heroes of that day: Thelma Armstrong, 54; John Bond, 77; Craig Hayden, 72; and William "Pat" Howard, 77. Members credit those eight minutes of terror, and the reactions inside them, with saving more than 200 lives, but describe a year since spent circling guilt and second-guessing. Many said the attack forced them into the hardest questions about suffering and where God is in a tragedy, and that telling their stories has become part of how the healing continues.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: New hymn ‘Peace, Peace, Be Still’ brings hope through the Savior to face life’s storms
item.description: Sally DeFord wrote the words to the new hymn "Peace, Peace, Be Still" while recovering from hand surgery, a trial she took at the time to be a hard one. Steeper ones followed, including multiple sclerosis, a daughter's cancer diagnosis and a recent stroke, sending her back to the refuge the lyrics describe in Jesus Christ, who rules the rising storm. Writing to the Church News on his wife's behalf, Dennis DeFord noted that the turmoil in each stanza softens and resolves into the Savior's command and invitation, echoing the psalm's call to be still and know that I am God. The full account is published at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: October 2026 general conference: How to watch, listen and follow
item.description: The 196th Semiannual General Conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints runs Oct. 3-4 with four sessions rather than five, the second conference held under the schedule the faith adjusted in fall 2025. Sessions start at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Mountain Daylight Time each day, last about two hours and originate from the Conference Center in Salt Lake City, with President Dallin H. Oaks presiding over all of them. Live coverage will run in more than 70 languages on broadcasts.ChurchofJesusChrist.org, alongside the General Conference YouTube channel in 14 languages, the Gospel Stream app in four and Gospel Library in 80. Bonneville Distribution handles satellite and broadcast carriage, including Dish Channel 9403, DirecTV channels 374 and 68 in Utah, BYUtv and KSL-TV Channel 5, while KSL NewsRadio airs the sessions on 102.7 FM and BYU Radio on SiriusXM Channel 143. In a recent letter to congregation leaders worldwide, the First Presidency framed conference as an opportunity to receive personal revelation and encouraged members to listen, study, ponder and apply the counsel given.

item.title: B’Nai Israel Temple religious legacy lives on in Salt Lake Art Museum
item.description: The former B'nai Israel Temple at 249 S. 400 East in Salt Lake City reopened on July 24 as the Salt Lake Art Museum, its first exhibit devoted to the synagogue's own history. Utah's Jewish story traces back to Fanny Brooks, who passed through Salt Lake City with her husband in 1854 and returned a decade later to settle at Third and Main; her children attended a Latter-day Saint Sunday School until the city had a synagogue of its own. Congregation B'nai Israel formed in 1873 and built near 300 South and West Temple, then split in 1885 into a Reform congregation and Congregation Montefiore, which moved from Orthodox to Conservative practice. The 400 East building was dedicated in July 1891 and served for more than 80 years before the two congregations merged as Kol Ami and sold it in 1976, after which it became a restaurant and later an office furniture showroom and headquarters for Henriksen Butler. Tour guide Kevin Earl, who researches the city's historic churches, said the exposed trusses over the gallery and nearly all the windows are original, and that Henriksen Butler's rear addition was built to meet accessibility standards without removing the original staircases.

item.title: Latter-day Saints around the world embrace new Sunday schedule
item.description: The revised Sunday schedule of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints compresses gospel instruction into 25-minute lesson blocks, and the Church News has been gathering members' reactions to teaching under it. Bobure Wabol, of the Bikenibeu 2nd Ward in the Tarawa Kiribati East Stake, wrote that the tighter window pushed her to settle on a single principle for each lesson rather than work through an entire assignment. She treats that constraint as a spiritual gain rather than a limitation, measuring a meeting by whether it strengthens faith in Jesus Christ. The full account is at TheChurchNews.com.
